key_insights: Distinguishes three application timing options: early programs (ED, restrictive EA, EA), rolling admission, and regular decision.
Early decision, restrictive early action, and early action generally share a due date around November 1st with decisions around mid-December, per the speaker.
Rolling admission schools generally return a decision about four to five weeks after materials are submitted, letting students lock in an acceptance earlier and adjust the rest of their list.
Recommends ED only for a student who has thoroughly researched the school (including checking its required net-price/financial-aid calculator) and is confident it is their genuine first choice.
States that in his experience, more financial aid money is typically still available in early rounds (ED, EA, rolling) than later in the regular decision cycle.
Early and rolling applications are evaluated without any senior-year coursework, so he recommends only applying early if freshman-junior year performance is already strong.
The main accepted way to exit a binding ED commitment is if the financial aid package doesn't work for the family, though the student is then typically out of that school's applicant pool.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Early round (ED/EA/REA) deadlines around November 1st with decisions around December 15th, per Sean
Regular decision deadlines typically January into February with decisions by mid-March, per Sean
Rolling admission decisions typically returned within about four to five weeks of a complete application, per Sean
notable_or_distinctive: Frames rolling admission as a distinct third strategic lane (beyond binding ED and non-binding EA), useful for students confident in their 9th-11th grade record who want an early answer without a binding commitment.
reliability_notes: This is an old video (published roughly 12 years ago per the channel listing), so claims about financial aid being more available in early rounds and other admissions norms may be dated; the speaker's credentials and institutional affiliation are not stated beyond a first name.
